🧬 Ovarian Teratoma
Ovarian teratoma spans mature cystic teratoma (dermoid), immature teratoma, and monodermal teratoma. The core radiologic task is to recognize teratomatous tissue - especially fat, hair, sebaceous material, and calcified tooth/bone - then assess for torsion, rupture/inflammation, or malignant behavior.
Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis
🗂️ Summary
  • Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid) is the most common ovarian neoplasm in Core and is usually benign.
  • Core notes a terminology boundary: a teratoma technically contains all three primitive germ cell layers, while a dermoid cyst may contain only two; in general use the terms are interchangeable.
  • The Rokitansky nodule is a mural protuberance from which hair commonly arises; teeth or bone, when present, are typically located in this protuberance.
🧭 Subtype / Risk Framework
  • Mature cystic teratoma: common benign dermoid pattern dominated by macroscopic fat, hair, sebaceous material, and/or calcified elements.
  • Immature teratoma: malignant germ cell tumor of younger patients; typically large, predominantly solid, irregular and heterogeneous, with small fat foci, coarse calcification, hemorrhage, and possible ascites or gliomatosis peritonei.
  • Monodermal teratoma: tissue from one dominant lineage; struma ovarii is composed predominantly of thyroid tissue and may have little or no fat.
🔍 Key Imaging Findings
Ultrasound
  • Classic mature dermoid clues include an echogenic shadowing Rokitansky nodule, linear or dot-dash hair echoes, fat-fluid level, highly echogenic fat, tooth-like calcification with posterior shadowing, and tip-of-the-iceberg attenuation.
  • Internal dermoid contents usually show no true Doppler flow; calcified components may create twinkling artifact, so pulsed Doppler confirmation matters.
CT
  • Macroscopic fat in an adnexal mass makes the diagnosis straightforward; tooth-like or coarse calcification further supports mature cystic teratoma.
MR Imaging
  • Macroscopic fat is T1 hyperintense and loses signal on fat-suppressed images. This separates a dermoid from an endometrioma, which can also be T1 bright but does not suppress as fat.
Nuclear Medicine
  • Immature teratoma and malignant components may show increased FDG uptake and higher SUVmax than mature cystic teratoma; Core also notes that functioning thyroid tissue may rarely be seen in an ovarian teratoma (struma ovarii).
⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Hemorrhagic cyst: fine fibrin strands and posterior enhancement favor hemorrhage; definite fat, a dermoid plug, tooth/calcification, hair echoes, or a fat-fluid level favor teratoma.
  • Endometrioma: homogeneous low-level internal echoes and failure to suppress on fat-saturated MRI favor endometrioma.
  • Pelvic abscess can mimic an inflamed dermoid; internal fat or calcified teratomatous elements preserve the clue to dermoid composition.
  • Bowel containing echogenic fecal material can mimic a dermoid on ultrasound; transvaginal localization, repeat scanning, bowel behavior, or MRI can clarify.
⚠️ Pearls / Pitfalls
  • Dermoids can act as lead points for adnexal torsion; Core emphasizes this particularly when the lesion is larger than 4 cm. Preserved Doppler flow does not exclude torsion because the ovary has dual arterial supply.
  • Rupture is uncommon but can release fatty/sebaceous material into the peritoneum and cause chemical peritonitis.
  • Malignant degeneration is rare; risk rises with older age, large tumors greater than about 10 cm, and rapid growth. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignant degeneration described by the fused source.
  • Approximately 10-20% of dermoids are bilateral, so the contralateral ovary should be inspected.
  • RadPrimer/STATdx note a rare association with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis; Core more broadly lists ovarian teratoma among malignancies associated with paraneoplastic autoimmune encephalitis.
✅ Super Summary
  • Fat + hair + tooth/calcification + Rokitansky nodule = mature cystic teratoma until proven otherwise; then confirm fat, inspect the opposite ovary, and search for torsion or suspicious solid vascular tissue.

column11: What tissue architecture explains the Rokitansky nodule, hair echoes, and tooth/bone calcification in a mature cystic teratoma?
column12: Mature cystic teratoma contains mature tissues derived from germ-cell lineages. The Rokitansky nodule is a true mural protuberance into the cyst cavity; most hair arises from it, and teeth or bone, when present, are typically located within the protuberance. The architecture therefore directly explains why a single ovarian lesion can look simultaneously cystic, echogenic, shadowing, fatty, and calcified.
